_note: Content engine pools (ENGINE_SPEC.md §14). Each post joins ONE scene to ONE teaching from its bucket's pool. Every tid must pass insight.ontology.citable(); the engine re-checks at pick time. 'point' is the teaching's own point (≤25 words); 'angle' is reader-facing and may appear in posts (≤30 words, one carousel slide). Scenes are invented, generic and free of personal data; each works as a post's first sentence. 'never' lists bucket-specific bans on top of rules/forbidden_claims.json, rules/tone.md and rules/content/originality.md.

buckets.name: Work pressure and burnout
buckets.audience: Working people carrying long days, full inboxes and the weight of results, who want an old, steady way to look at the work in front of them.
scenes: An email marked urgent lands at 10:40 at night.
The to-do list is longer at six in the evening than it was at nine.
A colleague presents your idea in the meeting as their own.
The laptop comes along on the family holiday, just in case.
Review week, and the form asks you to describe your impact.
Back-to-back calls, and lunch is eaten standing at the desk.
One more project gets a yes before the last one is done.
A report goes out to the whole team with a mistake on page two.
The promotion goes to someone else.
A project you cared about is cancelled after six months.
Sunday evening, and Monday has already started in your head.
A message from the manager: 'Quick call?' and nothing more.
A sharp reply sits in the drafts folder, cursor blinking.
Praise in the team meeting, and the wish to hear it again tomorrow.
A new colleague asks how the system works, on the busiest day of the month.

teaching_pool.point: Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna his right is to the action alone, never to its fruits, and not to cling to inaction either.
teaching_pool.angle: The work is in your hands; how it is received never was. The verse also closes the other door: dropping the work is not its answer.

teaching_pool.point: Act without clinging, Kṛṣṇa says, the same in success and failure; that sameness (samatva) is called yoga.
teaching_pool.angle: Before the result comes in, the verse asks for one thing: to do the work the same way whether it lands or not.

teaching_pool.point: Yoga, the Gītā says, is skill in actions (karmasu kauśalam), for one whose understanding is held steady.
teaching_pool.angle: In the verse, skill belongs to understanding held steady while acting. It speaks of how the work is done, not how much of it gets done.

teaching_pool.point: Do your allotted work (niyataṃ karma), Kṛṣṇa says; action is better than inaction, and even keeping the body going needs it.
teaching_pool.angle: The verse asks for allotted work, not all the work there is. On a day of forty requests, that one word, allotted, is worth sitting with.

teaching_pool.point: Always without attachment, do the work that has to be done, Kṛṣṇa says; acting unattached, a person reaches the highest.
teaching_pool.angle: The task list stays the same. What the verse changes is the grip: the work that has to be done, done without holding on to it.

teaching_pool.point: Free of attachment to results, ever content, depending on nothing, such a person does nothing at all, the Gītā says, even while fully busy.
teaching_pool.angle: A full calendar and an unclenched mind are not opposites in this verse. The busyness is outside; what it asks for is the not-clinging inside.

teaching_pool.point: Content with what comes unasked, free of envy, the same in success and failure, such a person acts and is not bound.
teaching_pool.angle: When a colleague's win stings, notice what the verse sets side by side: freedom from envy (vimatsara) and contentment with what comes.

teaching_pool.point: One who acts without clinging, offering the work to Brahman, is not stained, the Gītā says, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.
teaching_pool.angle: The lotus leaf sits in the pond all day. The image is not about leaving the water; it is about how the water runs off.

teaching_pool.point: The true renouncer and yogin, Kṛṣṇa says, is one who does the work to be done without depending on its fruit.
teaching_pool.angle: No retreat is needed for this. The verse finds renunciation inside ordinary work: doing it without leaning on what it will bring back.

teaching_pool.point: Kṛṣṇa praises one who is capable (dakṣa), pure and impartial, who expects nothing, is rid of distress and relinquishes every undertaking.
teaching_pool.angle: Capable and expecting nothing sit in the same verse. Being good at the work and not needing it to pay you back are held together.

teaching_pool.point: The one dear to Kṛṣṇa is the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, in cold and heat, pleasure and pain.
teaching_pool.angle: Praise on Monday, criticism on Thursday. The verse lists honour and dishonour right beside cold and heat, and asks for the same evenness toward both.

teaching_pool.point: The Gītā counts as austerity of speech words that cause no agitation and are truthful, pleasant and beneficial.
teaching_pool.angle: Before sending the sharp reply, the verse offers a four-part test: does it agitate, is it true, is it pleasant to hear, does it help?

teaching_pool.point: The Gītā's steady doer is free of clinging and ego, full of steadiness and zeal, and unchanged by success or failure.
teaching_pool.angle: Steadiness (dhṛti) and zeal (utsāha) appear together here. Keen about the work and unmoved by how it turns out: the verse wants both at once.

teaching_pool.point: Practice becomes firmly grounded, the Yoga Sūtra says, when kept up for a long time, without a break, and with care (satkāra).
teaching_pool.angle: The sutra's measure is long time, no gaps and care. Intensity is not on its list, so a few quiet minutes kept daily fit it well.

teaching_pool.point: From contentment (saṃtoṣa), the Yoga Sūtra says, comes unsurpassed happiness.
teaching_pool.angle: The raise, the title, the next target: the sutra does not put the highest happiness at the end of that list. It names contentment instead.

teaching_pool.point: Posture is mastered, the Yoga Sūtra says, by relaxing effort (prayatna-śaithilya) and by resting the mind on the endless.
teaching_pool.angle: Even the sitting posture of yoga is reached by easing effort, not piling it on. A line worth remembering at a desk held tight all day.

teaching_pool.point: The Visuddhimagga names gain as an impediment (palibodha): a monk so busy receiving and thanking has no time for his real work.
teaching_pool.angle: Even good things can crowd out what matters. The text's word is impediment: not a fault, just something that leaves no time.

teaching_pool.point: A crowd of pupils can be an impediment too, the Visuddhimagga says, when teaching them leaves a teacher no time for his own practice.
teaching_pool.angle: Being needed by many is named plainly here as something that can use up the day. The text's advice: finish what is nearly done, then step away.

teaching_pool.point: Returning anger to an angry man is worse, the Buddha's verse says; not returning it, one wins a battle hard to win.
teaching_pool.angle: The sharp remark in the meeting has already happened. The verse is about the next move: not handing the anger back, which it counts as the harder victory.

teaching_pool.point: When resentment will not settle, the Visuddhimagga asks what anger will achieve, and recalls that each person owns and inherits their own deeds (kamma).
teaching_pool.angle: Replaying a colleague's slight on the way home, the text's question is practical: what will this anger actually do, and whose deed is it?

teaching_pool.point: The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta asks for clear knowing (sampajāna) in every ordinary act: going and returning, eating, speaking and keeping silent.
teaching_pool.angle: The walk to the next meeting belongs to the practice in this sutta, not to the gap between tasks. It asks only for knowing the walk while it happens.

teaching_pool.point: The Tattvārtha says the weight of an act differs by intensity or mildness, and by whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly.
teaching_pool.angle: The error in the report was not made knowingly. The Jain text weighs an act by intent and intensity, not only by how it looks from outside.

teaching_pool.point: Spite, hiding what one knows, envy and blocking others' learning, the Tattvārtha says, bring in karma that clouds one's own knowledge.
teaching_pool.angle: Keeping the handover notes vague so no one else can do the job: the Jain text counts that as clouding the hider's own knowing, not only the others'.

teaching_pool.point: Few undertakings (ārambha) and little possessiveness, the Tattvārtha says, are what bring in the karma of a human life.
teaching_pool.angle: Saying yes to every new project is what this text calls undertaking. It links a human life with fewer of them, and with holding loosely to what one owns.

teaching_pool.point: Among the causes of the highest karma, a Tīrthaṅkara's, the Tattvārtha lists giving and austerity according to one's own power (śaktitaḥ).
teaching_pool.angle: Even in a list of the highest virtues, the measure is one's own strength. The sutra asks for effort that fits your power, not someone else's.

teaching_pool.point: Censuring others, praising oneself, hiding others' real virtues and claiming false ones, the Tattvārtha says, bring in low-status karma.
teaching_pool.angle: The meeting where credit is quietly re-routed: the Jain text names each move in it, and says the cost falls on the one who makes them.

teaching_pool.point: To keep speech truthful, the Tattvārtha asks one to give up anger, greed, fear and joking.
teaching_pool.angle: The Jain text guards truth at its sources. Before the quick reply goes out, it asks which of four is speaking: anger, greed, fear or the joke.

never: Productivity or performance promises: never say a teaching makes anyone faster, more productive, more focused or better at a job.
Burnout, stress or exhaustion as a condition or label for the reader; describe the scene instead (long days, too much, running on empty).
Career predictions: nothing about promotions, raises, job offers, layoffs or how a review will go.
Advice to quit, stay, confront a manager, or take legal or HR steps.
Company, product, app or brand names, and any detail that could identify a real workplace or person.
Using the Gītā's battlefield setting as licence for conflict at work, or svadharma and caste duty as a reason to accept mistreatment.
Recommending austerity (tapas) or fasting; the 'according to one's power' of TS 6.24 is never turned into a call for more effort.
Hustle framing ('grind', 'crush it', 'no days off') or praise of overwork; equally, no scorn for ambition.

buckets.name: Anxiety and overthinking
buckets.audience: People whose minds keep going over things: replaying conversations, rehearsing what might happen, reopening decisions already made.
scenes: A message shows 'seen', and no reply comes.
On the drive home, the meeting replays with better lines each time.
A comment from three years ago comes back while brushing your teeth.
Twelve browser tabs open, each one a different worry.
Twenty minutes spent drafting a two-line text.
Before a trip, everything that could go wrong gets its own rehearsal.
A friend's short reply gets read five different ways.
In the shower, an argument that may never happen is rehearsed again.
Waiting for an exam result, the mind runs ahead to every outcome.
Scrolling back through an old chat to find where it went wrong.
The decision is made, and the mind keeps reopening it.
A small slip at work grows larger with each replay.
Stuck at a red light, planning three conversations at once.
Someone's slightly cold tone, and the whole afternoon goes to it.
A week of choosing between two options, and still no choice.

teaching_pool.point: Yoga, the Yoga Sūtra says, is the stilling (nirodha) of the mind's activities (vṛtti).
teaching_pool.angle: The sutra does not ask for an empty mind by force. It names the churning as activity, something that moves, and so something that can be stilled.

teaching_pool.point: At other times, the Yoga Sūtra says, the seer takes on the form of the mind's activities (sārūpya).
teaching_pool.angle: The tenth replay of the same conversation, in the sutra's terms: the one who sees starts to look like the thought being seen.

teaching_pool.point: Memory (smṛti), the Yoga Sūtra says, is the not-slipping-away of something once experienced.
teaching_pool.angle: The old remark that keeps returning is memory doing what the sutra says memory does: not letting the experienced thing slip. It is named, not blamed.

teaching_pool.point: The mind's activities are stilled, the Yoga Sūtra says, by practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya) together.
teaching_pool.angle: Two means, not one: coming back again and again, and not feeding the thing the mind keeps reaching for.

teaching_pool.point: Practice (abhyāsa), the Yoga Sūtra says, is the effort toward stability.
teaching_pool.angle: Practice here is not a score to hit. It is the effort to stay, and then to stay again after drifting off.

teaching_pool.point: To remove the mind's distractions, the Yoga Sūtra advises practice on a single principle (eka-tattva).
teaching_pool.angle: When the mind runs down twelve paths at once, the sutra's counsel is one: choose a single thing and keep returning to it.

teaching_pool.point: When harmful thoughts (vitarka) press in, the Yoga Sūtra says, cultivate their opposite.
teaching_pool.angle: Rehearsing a cutting reply to someone who did you wrong is one such thought. The sutra's counsel is to grow the opposite thought, deliberately.

teaching_pool.point: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, Kṛṣṇa says, bring it back from there.
teaching_pool.angle: No verdict on the wandering. The whole instruction in this verse is the return, from wherever the mind went, as often as it goes.

teaching_pool.point: Arjuna says the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn; holding it seems as hard as holding the wind.
teaching_pool.angle: The Gītā lets its hero say it first and plainly. The complaint about a mind that will not stop is already in the text.

teaching_pool.point: Kṛṣṇa grants that the mind is restless and hard to hold, then says it is held by practice and dispassion.
teaching_pool.angle: He does not argue with Arjuna's complaint. He agrees with it first, then names the two means. Agreement, then method.

teaching_pool.point: Little by little one should come to rest, Kṛṣṇa says, the mind settled in the self, thinking of nothing at all.
teaching_pool.angle: The phrase 'little by little' (śanaiḥ śanaiḥ) matters. The verse does not demand a quiet mind at once; it describes a slow settling.

teaching_pool.point: Dwelling on objects breeds attachment, the Gītā says; from attachment desire is born, and from desire, anger.
teaching_pool.angle: The chain starts with dwelling: the fifth look at the same message, the tenth replay. The verse places the start there, well before the anger.

teaching_pool.point: When the mind follows the roving senses, the Gītā says, it carries off understanding as the wind carries a ship on water.
teaching_pool.angle: Notification, tab, another tab. The verse's image is a boat with no anchor, blown wherever the senses go next.

teaching_pool.point: A mind held steady, the Gītā says, is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker.
teaching_pool.angle: The image is not of a lamp put out, but of one still burning. The mind stays lit; only the wind drops.

teaching_pool.point: Dear to Kṛṣṇa is one who does not disturb the world and is not disturbed by it, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation.
teaching_pool.angle: The verse runs both ways: not shaken by the world, and not shaking it. The group chat, seen from both ends.

teaching_pool.point: Restraining the mind, Gauḍapāda says, is like emptying the ocean drop by drop with a blade of grass, done without weariness.
teaching_pool.angle: The image admits the size of the task. Its instruction is about manner: drop by drop, and without wearing yourself out (aparikheda).

teaching_pool.point: When the mind sinks, Gauḍapāda says, rouse it; when it scatters, calm it; when it reaches evenness, do not stir it.
teaching_pool.angle: The last line is easy to miss: once the mind is even, leave it be. Leaving it alone is part of the instruction.

teaching_pool.point: When restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) are present, the Satipaṭṭhāna says, one knows they are present, how they arise and how they go.
teaching_pool.angle: The first step here is not to stop the worry but to know it is there. The sutta's words are simple: 'there is restlessness in me.'

teaching_pool.point: The Satipaṭṭhāna asks one to know a scattered mind as scattered, and a collected mind as collected.
teaching_pool.angle: No fixing in this line. Seeing the scattered mind as 'scattered' is itself the practice the sutta describes.

teaching_pool.point: Counting breaths, the Visuddhimagga says, has one purpose: to set mindfulness on the breath by cutting off thoughts scattered outside.
teaching_pool.angle: The counting is scaffolding. Once mindfulness stands on the breath, the text says, the counting is dropped. A tool, not a target.

teaching_pool.point: For one whose thoughts run about, the Visuddhimagga says, a wide view feeds the running; a small object suits better.
teaching_pool.angle: The text is practical: a sweeping view gives racing thoughts more to chase. It advises a sheltered place and a small object.

teaching_pool.point: With each breath, the Ānāpānasati Sutta trains one in experiencing the mind, gladdening it, collecting it and freeing it.
teaching_pool.angle: Before any freeing comes experiencing the mind as it is, busy or not. The sutta starts there, with the breath going in and out.

teaching_pool.point: With nothing to attain, the Heart Sūtra says, the mind has no obstruction; with no obstruction there is no fear, and no upside-down thinking.
teaching_pool.angle: The sutra traces fear to obstruction in the mind, and obstruction to reaching for something to gain. The chain runs back to 'nothing to attain'.

teaching_pool.point: Among the supports of non-violence, the Tattvārtha lists restraint of speech and restraint of mind (mano-gupti), with care in walking and handling things.
teaching_pool.angle: The Jain text puts guarding the mind beside guarding speech. The unsent angry message and the one rehearsed in the head sit on the same list.

teaching_pool.point: Intense states of mind driven by the passions (kaṣāya), the Tattvārtha says, bring in karma that clouds right conduct.
teaching_pool.angle: The Jain text looks at intensity (tīvra) itself: how hot a state of mind runs matters, not only what it is about.

teaching_pool.point: In the Tattvārtha, karma's fruit is its being experienced, and from that experiencing comes its shedding (nirjarā).
teaching_pool.angle: In this Jain account, what ripens is felt, and in being felt it falls away. The text names that falling away as shedding.

never: The word 'anxiety' or 'anxious' as a condition to be treated, calmed or managed; speak of worry, a mind that will not stop, going over things.
Any promise that a teaching or practice will stop, calm, fix or quieten worrying thoughts.
Clinical or brain words: disorder, panic attack, OCD, nervous system, the brain, rumination as a technical term.
Breath work beyond plain awareness of the breath as the suttas and the Visuddhimagga describe it; never breath retention of any kind.
Telling a reader their worries are unreal, an illusion or a dream; the non-dual teachings are never used to dismiss a worry.
Scenes about medical tests, health scares, or repeated checking of locks and switches.
Listicle or hack framing ('stop overthinking in 3 steps').
Suggesting anyone stop or replace professional help.

buckets.name: Sleep
buckets.audience: People who meet the night awake, wake with the day already in their heads, or wonder what sleep and dreams are, looking for reflection rather than tips.
scenes: It is 3 a.m., and the ceiling is very familiar.
The alarm rings, and the first thought is the inbox.
A dream hangs around all through breakfast.
One more episode, and then one more.
The phone's light on a face in a dark room, long after midnight.
Waking before the alarm, in the quiet before the house stirs.
A heavy hour at the desk after lunch.
The night bus home, half-asleep against the window.
A baby's cry at 2 a.m., then the long walk back to bed.
Lying down, and the day's conversations start up again.
Sunday morning with nowhere to be, and still awake at six.
A nap that ran two hours, and waking unsure what day it is.
Night shift over, going to bed as the city wakes.
The first sound on waking: birds, traffic, or rain.
Someone breathing slowly, asleep in the next room.

teaching_pool.point: Yoga is not for one who eats too much or not at all, the Gītā says, nor for one who sleeps too much or too little.
teaching_pool.angle: The verse names both ends and sets no hours. It is a verse about measure, not a rule to keep.

teaching_pool.point: The Gītā asks for measure (yukta) in food and recreation, in effort at work, and in sleep and waking alike.
teaching_pool.angle: Sleep sits in a list with meals, leisure and work. The verse does not single it out; it asks for the same measure across the whole day.

teaching_pool.point: What is night for all beings, the Gītā says, the self-restrained one is awake in; what they wake to is night for the sage.
teaching_pool.angle: The verse is not about staying up. It turns night and waking into a question: what are you awake to, and what goes unseen by day?

teaching_pool.point: Even while seeing, walking, sleeping and breathing, the Gītā says, one who knows the truth thinks, 'I do nothing at all.'
teaching_pool.angle: Sleep appears here in a plain list of what the body does. Lying down at night, the verse offers a thought: not all the doing is yours.

teaching_pool.point: Sleep (nidrā), the Yoga Sūtra says, is an activity of the mind whose support is the cognition of absence.
teaching_pool.angle: In this sutra sleep is not the mind switched off. It is one of the mind's five activities, with absence as its object.

teaching_pool.point: Vyāsa notes that on waking one says 'I slept well, my mind is clear' or 'I slept heavily, my mind is dull'.
teaching_pool.angle: Those first words of the morning are, for Vyāsa, evidence: remembering the night at all shows that sleep was itself a kind of cognition.

teaching_pool.point: The mind may also be steadied, the Yoga Sūtra says, by taking the knowledge of dream or of sleep as its support.
teaching_pool.angle: The sutra places dream and sleep among the things a steady mind can rest on in reflection. The night becomes material for daytime attention.

teaching_pool.point: The first quarter of the self, the Māṇḍūkya says, is waking: knowing outward and enjoying the gross world.
teaching_pool.angle: Waking here is one station among four, not the whole of what a person is. The Upaniṣad starts its map of the self with the ordinary morning.

teaching_pool.point: The second quarter, the Māṇḍūkya says, is dream: knowing inward, enjoying a world set apart.
teaching_pool.angle: The Upaniṣad neither dismisses dreams nor reads them as omens. It gives dream its own station in the self, facing inward.

teaching_pool.point: Where one asleep wants nothing and sees no dream, the Māṇḍūkya says, that is deep sleep: one, a mass of knowing, made of bliss.
teaching_pool.angle: The Upaniṣad describes deep sleep as unified, not empty. It is a description of a state, not a promise about any night.

teaching_pool.point: When the being asleep in beginningless illusion (māyā) awakens, Gauḍapāda says, it wakes to the unborn: sleepless, dreamless, non-dual.
teaching_pool.angle: Here waking is a word for understanding, not for the alarm clock. The text borrows the night to speak of a larger waking.

teaching_pool.point: In deep sleep the mind is absorbed, Gauḍapāda says; the restrained mind is not absorbed, and that is fearless brahman.
teaching_pool.angle: The text separates the two with care: both are still, but deep sleep is not the goal it points to. The difference is the light of knowing.

teaching_pool.point: When one sleeps, the Chāndogya says, one has gone to one's own; like a tethered bird, the mind settles in breath.
teaching_pool.angle: The bird flies every way before it settles at its post. The Upaniṣad describes sleep as going home, not as a task to get right.

teaching_pool.point: Taught that the self is the one in dreamless sleep, Indra objects: there one does not know oneself as 'I am he'.
teaching_pool.angle: Not every Upaniṣad voice praises deep sleep. Indra finds a flaw in it and keeps asking. The texts differ here, and say so.

teaching_pool.point: As a tired falcon folds its wings for its nest, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says, one goes where, asleep, nothing is wanted and no dream seen.
teaching_pool.angle: The image is of a bird that has flown all day. Rest is described as the nest the flying was always returning to.

teaching_pool.point: In dream, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says, the person takes material from this world, breaks it up, builds it again, and becomes his own light.
teaching_pool.angle: The strange buildings of a dream are, in this text, made by the dreamer's own light. It marvels at the maker rather than decoding the dream.

teaching_pool.point: The person awake in those who sleep, shaping desire after desire: that, the Kaṭha says, is the bright, the immortal.
teaching_pool.angle: While the body sleeps, the text says, someone is awake. It speaks of that one with reverence, not as a problem to solve.

teaching_pool.point: That by which one perceives both dream and waking: knowing it as the great self, the Kaṭha says, the wise do not grieve.
teaching_pool.angle: Dream and waking have one witness in this verse. Crossing from one to the other at dawn, the text asks who sees both.

teaching_pool.point: Arise, awake, the Kaṭha says; having obtained the boons, understand. The path is sharp as a razor's edge, hard to cross.
teaching_pool.angle: The morning call here is to understanding, and the text does not pretend it is easy: a razor's edge, it says.

teaching_pool.point: In dreamless sleep speech, sight, hearing and mind go into breath, the Kauṣītaki says; on waking they fly out like sparks from a fire.
teaching_pool.angle: Morning, in this image, is sparks leaving one fire: the senses going back out into the day from a single source.

teaching_pool.point: The Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna asks for clear knowing (sampajāna) in every act, including falling asleep and waking up.
teaching_pool.angle: Falling asleep is on the sutta's list beside eating and walking. Nothing special is asked of it, only that it be known.

teaching_pool.point: When lying down, the Satipaṭṭhāna says, one knows 'I am lying down'; however the body is placed, one knows it.
teaching_pool.angle: The sutta's instruction for lying down is one line long: know the lying down. No technique, no target.

teaching_pool.point: When dullness and drowsiness (thina-middha) are present, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna says, one knows they are present, and how they come and go.
teaching_pool.angle: The heavy hour after lunch is named here, not blamed. The sutta asks only for knowing: 'dullness and drowsiness are here.'

teaching_pool.point: The Tattvārtha lists kinds of sleep and drowsiness among the karmas that veil perception (darśana-āvaraṇa).
teaching_pool.angle: The Jain text names the grades of sleep with care, from dozing to deep sleep, and files them all under what veils seeing. It describes; it does not scold.

never: Any statement or hint that a teaching, verse or practice improves sleep, helps anyone fall or stay asleep, or makes rest deeper or better.
Condition and hygiene words: insomnia, sleep disorder, sleep hygiene; no advice on hours, bedtimes, naps, screens or routines.
Dream interpretation, dream omens or predictions from dreams; no sleep charms or protective rites (the Atharvaveda hymn to Sleep is not used).
The Visuddhimagga's list of the benefits of loving-kindness ('sleeps in comfort, wakes in comfort') is not used in this account.
Verses that place sleep under dullness (tamas), such as BhG 14.8 and 18.39, are not used to judge anyone's sleep or rest.
Presenting deep sleep as the goal the texts point to, or promising the bliss the Māṇḍūkya describes.
Breathing or meditation instructions framed as something to do in bed to get to sleep.
Any mention of sleeping pills, supplements or medicine, for or against.

buckets.name: Loneliness
buckets.audience: People who spend more evenings alone than they would choose, or feel alone among others, and would welcome the company of old words.
scenes: Dinner for one, with a show on for the sound of voices.
The group chat moves on, and your message stays unanswered.
A new city, and no one at the shop knows your name.
A birthday with more notifications than visitors.
Working from home, and the only voice all day is your own.
A crowded train, and not one pair of eyes meets yours.
Photos of a party that no one mentioned.
The phone lights up, and it is only an app.
An old friend's number, and not knowing what to say after so long.
Sunday afternoon, with the week's plans all cancelled.
Lunch at the desk while the others go out together.
A festival evening, and the streets full of families.
Coming home to a quiet flat and switching every light on.
A neighbour's window where people are laughing.
Saying 'I'm fine' three times in one day.

teaching_pool.point: Lift yourself by yourself, Kṛṣṇa says, and do not let yourself sink; the self alone is the self's friend, and its enemy.
teaching_pool.angle: The verse names a friend who is there when no one else is. It is honest that the same self can also act as an enemy.

teaching_pool.point: One yoked in yoga, the Gītā says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self.
teaching_pool.angle: On a crowded train where no eyes meet, the verse describes a way of seeing: the same self looking out through every face.

teaching_pool.point: Whoever sees me everywhere and everything in me, Kṛṣṇa says, I am not lost to him, and he is not lost to me.
teaching_pool.angle: This is a devotional verse, and its closeness is with the divine. Its words are about not being lost, a kind of company the text offers plainly.

teaching_pool.point: The highest yogin, the Gītā says, sees others' pleasure and pain by likeness to himself (ātmaupamya).
teaching_pool.angle: The ache of an empty evening becomes, in this verse, the measure for noticing someone else's. One's own pain is how another's is known.

teaching_pool.point: Their thought on the Lord, the Gītā says, devotees awaken one another (bodhayantaḥ parasparam), speak of him, and are content and glad.
teaching_pool.angle: Company in this verse is not small talk. It is people waking each other up to what matters most to them, and finding delight in it.

teaching_pool.point: Dear to Kṛṣṇa is one who hates no being, is friendly and compassionate, free of 'mine' and 'I', and forbearing.
teaching_pool.angle: Friendliness (maitra) here is not a reward for having friends. It is a way of facing every being, including those who have not reached out.

teaching_pool.point: The Gītā counts resorting to secluded places, and finding no delight in crowds, among the marks of knowledge.
teaching_pool.angle: Solitude and loneliness are not the same. The Gītā speaks only of the first, chosen and quiet, and gives it a place on the path.

teaching_pool.point: Seers whose doubts are cut, self-restrained and delighting in the welfare of all beings, the Gītā says, reach the peace of Brahman.
teaching_pool.angle: The delight named here is taken in the welfare of all beings, strangers included. It is a joy that faces outward.

teaching_pool.point: The mind grows clear, the Yoga Sūtra says, through friendliness to the happy, compassion for the suffering, gladness for the virtuous, equanimity toward the unvirtuous.
teaching_pool.angle: The sutra gives each kind of person an attitude of its own. Friendliness goes to the happy, compassion to those who struggle.

teaching_pool.point: Alone in the beginning, the first being was afraid, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says; then it asked: with nothing but me, what is there to fear?
teaching_pool.angle: The Upaniṣad begins creation with someone alone and afraid. The fear is taken seriously, then questioned from the inside.

teaching_pool.point: He found no delight, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says; one who is alone finds no delight. He wanted a second.
teaching_pool.angle: The Upaniṣad says it without embarrassment: alone, there was no delight, and the wish for a second is where its world begins.

teaching_pool.point: One who sees all beings in the self and the self in all beings, the Īśa says, shrinks from nothing.
teaching_pool.angle: The verse's word is 'shrinks from' (vijugupsate). It describes a seeing in which no one is a stranger to recoil from.

teaching_pool.point: It is a vow, the Taittirīya says, never to turn away one who seeks lodging; so gather plenty of food.
teaching_pool.angle: The vow runs outward. Before any question of being visited, it asks for an open door and food ready for whoever comes.

teaching_pool.point: Given three boons by Death, Naciketas first asks that his father be calm and kind, and welcome him home.
teaching_pool.angle: Offered a wish by Death himself, the boy's first request is to be welcomed back. The Upaniṣad puts that longing first.

teaching_pool.point: Loving-kindness, the Visuddhimagga says, is first developed toward oneself: 'may I be happy and free from suffering.'
teaching_pool.angle: The text puts oneself first in the order, not last. Friendliness begins where you already sit, even on a night alone.

teaching_pool.point: Wishing oneself happy, the Visuddhimagga says, one sees: as I want happiness and dislike suffering, so do other beings.
teaching_pool.angle: Your own wish to be happy becomes, in this text, the bridge to the wishes of all other beings. Your own wanting is the witness.

teaching_pool.point: Loving-kindness is developed toward oneself, a dear person, a neutral person and an enemy, the Visuddhimagga says, until the barriers between them break.
teaching_pool.angle: The stranger at the bus stop is the 'neutral person' of this text. The practice gives them the same place as a dear friend, and as oneself.

teaching_pool.point: Gladness (muditā), the Visuddhimagga says, has rejoicing as its mark, not envying as its function, and it removes discontent.
teaching_pool.angle: Scrolling through others' celebrations alone, the text's word is gladness. Its mark is rejoicing; its work is not envying.

teaching_pool.point: The near enemy of compassion, the Visuddhimagga says, is worldly grief over what is lacking or lost: it too sees what has gone wrong.
teaching_pool.angle: Missing what one had can look like compassion, the text says, because both see what has gone wrong. It keeps the two apart.

teaching_pool.point: The Buddha praises an assembly without chatter or idle talk, settled on what is essential: rare, and worth travelling far to see.
teaching_pool.angle: The sutta's picture of good company is quiet: people gathered without chatter, settled on what matters, and praised as rare.

teaching_pool.point: The Tattvārtha asks for friendliness toward all living beings, delight in the virtuous, compassion for the afflicted, equanimity toward the unruly.
teaching_pool.angle: The Jain list starts with friendliness toward all living beings (sattva), not only people one knows. The circle is drawn as wide as it goes.

teaching_pool.point: Compassion for living beings, giving, forbearance and purity, the Tattvārtha says, bring in karma of pleasant feeling.
teaching_pool.angle: In this Jain account, compassion and giving shape the one who offers them. Kindness sent outward does not only travel outward.

never: Promises of connection: never say a reader will find friends, love or a partner, or that loneliness will pass.
'You are never alone' or any line that tells the reader the feeling is wrong; teachings on oneness are given as the texts' view, not as a correction.
Clinical words (depression, isolation as a condition) or any link between loneliness and health.
Praising solitude to someone who did not choose it; BhG 13.11 is about chosen seclusion and is presented as such.
Crisis material: self-harm, suicide or abuse are never used as scenes; those belong to the safety messages, not to posts.
Dating, relationship or astrological compatibility content.
Devotional verses (BhG 6.30, 10.9) used to recruit or to suggest the reader should adopt a faith.
Pity or rescue language ('you poor thing', 'we are here for you') and any promise of a reply or a community.

buckets.name: Meaning and identity
buckets.audience: People at a turn in life, after a goal, a loss of role or a change of place, asking what their life is for and who they are without the labels.
scenes: At a party, someone asks, 'So, what do you do?'
The goal is reached, and the next morning feels flat.
A birthday ending in zero.
A form asks for 'occupation', a month after leaving the job.
The last child leaves home, and the house goes quiet.
An old diary full of plans that never happened.
The degree is framed on the wall, and the question 'what now?' remains.
A friend's life looks further along on the screen.
The new job title in the email signature does not sound like you.
Clearing out a wardrobe of clothes from another life.
The first Monday of retirement.
Standing in a quiet temple, not sure what to look for.
A childhood photo, and wondering who that was.
A move abroad, where no one knows who you used to be.
A choice between the safe offer and the one that feels right.

teaching_pool.point: Arjuna admits he is bewildered about what is right (dharma) and asks Kṛṣṇa to tell him plainly what is better.
teaching_pool.angle: The Gītā's teaching begins with someone who does not know what to do and says so. Not knowing is where the text starts, not where it fails.

teaching_pool.point: Arjuna says not even an unrivalled kingdom, not even rule over the gods, would drive away his grief.
teaching_pool.angle: The goal arrives and the hollowness stays. Arjuna says the same: no kingdom he can name would lift this grief.

teaching_pool.point: The self, the Gītā says, is not born and does not die; unborn and eternal, it is not killed when the body is killed.
teaching_pool.angle: A title, a role, a decade: each has a start date. The Gītā describes something in the person that has none. The Buddhist texts disagree, and say so.

teaching_pool.point: As a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the Gītā says, the embodied one passes from worn-out bodies to new ones.
teaching_pool.angle: The Gītā's picture of the self is someone changing clothes. What wears out, it says, is the garment, not the wearer.

teaching_pool.point: Actions are done by the qualities (guṇa) of nature, the Gītā says; one deluded by the sense of 'I' thinks, 'I am the doer.'
teaching_pool.angle: When a failure feels like a verdict on the whole person, the verse questions the 'I' at its centre: who, exactly, was the doer?

teaching_pool.point: Better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, Kṛṣṇa says, than another's done well; another's dharma brings danger.
teaching_pool.angle: Svadharma meant, in the Gītā, the duty of one's own station in life. Its point on the page still stands: one's own, done imperfectly, over another's done well.

teaching_pool.point: This body, Kṛṣṇa says, is called the field (kṣetra); the one who knows it is called the knower of the field.
teaching_pool.angle: The mirror shows the field. The verse points to the one looking: the knower of the field is not the same as what it knows.

teaching_pool.point: Having taught Arjuna the most secret knowledge, Kṛṣṇa says: reflect on it fully, then do as you wish.
teaching_pool.angle: At the end of the whole teaching, the teacher does not give orders. He hands the choice back: think it all through, then choose.

teaching_pool.point: Then, the Yoga Sūtra says, the seer abides in its own form (svarūpa).
teaching_pool.angle: Not a new identity to build, the sutra says, but the seer resting in its own form once the mind's activity is stilled.

teaching_pool.point: Ignorance (avidyā), the Yoga Sūtra says, takes the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, pain as pleasure and the not-self as self.
teaching_pool.angle: The last mistake on the list stings at a job change: taking what is not the self, a title or a role, for the self.

teaching_pool.point: I-am-ness (asmitā), the Yoga Sūtra says, is the seer and the instrument of seeing appearing to be one.
teaching_pool.angle: 'I am my job', 'I am my marks': the sutra names this blending of seer and instrument, and counts it among the afflictions.

teaching_pool.point: The good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) differ, the Kaṭha says; both come to a person, and the wise choose the good.
teaching_pool.angle: The pleasant offer and the good one rarely come labelled. The Upaniṣad asks that they be examined and told apart before choosing.

teaching_pool.point: Know the self as the rider in the chariot, the Kaṭha says: the body is the chariot, intellect the driver, mind the reins.
teaching_pool.angle: A picture for a life pulled many ways: the senses are the horses, the mind the reins, and someone is riding.

teaching_pool.point: Nārada had studied every science of his day, yet told Sanatkumāra: 'I know only the words, not the self; I am in sorrow.'
teaching_pool.angle: Degrees, skills, a full record of learning: Nārada had all of it and still came asking. The Upaniṣad makes his sorrow the start of learning.

teaching_pool.point: Asked by his son Bhṛgu to teach him brahman, Varuṇa says: seek to know that from which beings are born, live and return.
teaching_pool.angle: The father gives no ready answer, only a direction to look in. The question of what all this is for is handed back to the one asking.

teaching_pool.point: The Taittirīya describes the person as five selves, each within the last: made of food, of breath, of mind, of understanding, of bliss.
teaching_pool.angle: Asked who one is, most answers stop at the first layer. The Upaniṣad keeps going inward, past body and mind, to understanding and bliss.

teaching_pool.point: Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form, the Heart Sūtra says; emptiness is not other than form, nor form other than emptiness.
teaching_pool.angle: Unlike the Upaniṣads, the sutra finds no lasting self beneath the roles. Form itself is empty, it says, and emptiness is not somewhere else.

teaching_pool.point: The Satipaṭṭhāna asks one to see form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness each arising and passing away.
teaching_pool.angle: Instead of asking 'who am I?', the sutta watches what the 'I' is made of, and sees each part arise and pass.

teaching_pool.point: Mindful that 'there is a body' just enough for knowing, the Satipaṭṭhāna says, one abides independent, clinging to nothing in the world.
teaching_pool.angle: The sutta keeps the body in view without making it a self. Just enough mindfulness to know, and nothing grabbed onto.

teaching_pool.point: The meditator regards even bright experiences as 'not mine, not I, not my self', the Visuddhimagga says, and so does not waver.
teaching_pool.angle: Even the brightest states are met here with the same three phrases. In this text nothing, however good, is made into 'me'.

teaching_pool.point: Formations appear ever new and short-lived, the Visuddhimagga says: like a dewdrop at sunrise, a bubble on water, a line drawn on water.
teaching_pool.angle: The old job, the old city, the person of ten years ago: the text's images are dew, bubble and a line on water. Short-lived, and ever new.

teaching_pool.point: The Tattvārtha names being a soul (jīvatva) as an inherent state (pāriṇāmika), not one produced by karma.
teaching_pool.angle: Roles come and go with circumstance. In Jain terms, being a living soul is not one of them. Here the Jain and Buddhist texts part ways.

teaching_pool.point: The Tattvārtha asks for reflection on the nature of the world and of the body, to stir dread of endless rebirth (saṃvega) and detachment.
teaching_pool.angle: A birthday ending in zero can bring this on uninvited. The Jain text asks for it on purpose: look at the world and the body as they are.

teaching_pool.point: Wrong view, non-restraint, carelessness, the passions and activity, the Tattvārtha says, are the causes of bondage.
teaching_pool.angle: The Jain answer to 'what holds me back?' is a list of five, and wrong view (mithyādarśana) comes first: how one sees comes before what one does.

never: Telling a reader who they are ('you are pure awareness', 'you are the eternal self'); say what each text says about the self.
Blending self and no-self: the Upaniṣads, the Gītā, the Yoga Sūtra and the Jain texts affirm a self; the Buddhist texts deny a lasting self. Name the difference, never merge them.
Using svadharma (BhG 3.35) to endorse caste or to tell a reader to stay in a role, job or station.
Destiny, purpose or life-path predictions; astrology, kundali or any 'your calling awaits' framing.
Recommending austerity (tapas) or fasting, even where a passage mentions it (TU 3.1.1).
Pushing renunciation, a guru or a conversion; no telling a reader to leave work, family or home.
Self-help promises such as 'find your purpose' or 'become your best self'.
Grief after a death used as a scene; bereavement is not this account's material.
